subtopic: REVERSION OF ACTIVE SERVICE OFFICERS TO RESERVE FORCE STATUS
speechtext:
I desire now to answer the question of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), who inquired yesterday with regard to the retirement of officers in the Pacific command.
The statement that "500 officers are being retired from the active force in the Pacific command" is not accurate. The number from October 1 to February 29 was 115, and the number pending at that time was 35.
Officers are not being returned in groups to reserve force status. Each case is dealt with individually and on its merits.
There have, from October 1 to February 29, been retired 639 officers. That does not include 225 officers who have been retired since July 1943 as being over 60 years of age. The house will understand that this includes those retired from the Pacific command and all others as well. Some have been returned to reserve status at their own request; some have been returned as over age for overseas service, some as below medical category for overseas service. Others are returned to reserve status because no suitable employment can be found for them in the Canadian army.
Maple Products

Officers' survey and classification boards have been set up to deal with the disposal of officers. Each officer to be returned to reserve status -except those returned at their own request- gets notice of the intention to return him to reserve status, with the reasons upon which the recommendation is based. The notice is given to him by his commanding officer. He is advised that he may, if he so wishes, submit a statement within a period of 14 days from the notice, setting forth any reasons he might have why such recommendation should not be carried into effect. He is also advised by the notice that, if no such statement is received from him by his commanding officer within the 14 days, his commanding officer will forward his recommendation through the usual channels to national defence headquarters. It is also stated in the notice that, if the officer does not wish to submit any reasons against the recommendation, he should state so in writing.
Before notice of the intention to recommend return to reserve status is sent to the particular officer, he will probably have been interviewed by the officers' survey and classification board. If he has not, and expresses the wish to appear before them, he is given an opportunity of doing so and of giving the board all the reasons he can to show why he should not be returned to reserve status. The board has no authority to dispose of an officer. The board simply puts in a recommendation to the district officer commanding or the general officer commanding concerned.
All officers who are returned to reserve status under the procedure by notice which has just been described are paid rehabilitation grant.
RATIONING-USE FOR PRESERVING PURPOSES On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Acting Minister of Finance):
speechtext:
May I make an answer to the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce), who in a question he asked yesterday inquired whether consideration would be given to the immediate removal of restrictions on the purchase of maple syrup and maple sugar.
The answer is that when rationing became necessary for preserves and sweeteners because of greatly increased demands and definite shortages of some items such as canned fruits, it was necessary that the general pool of sweeteners be dealt with as a whole and that each consumer be given an equal claim upon it. It would have been discrimination in favour of consumers of maple syrup if they had been able to purchase their maple syrup [DOT]without coupons and still have all their coupons to purchase other sweeteners or the alternative of sugar. In dealing with rationed commodities it is the policy of the wartime prices and trade board to treat all parts of Canada equally and to avoid discrimination in favour of any particular section or group of consumers. Accordingly as at present advised it is not the intention to remove maple syrup or maple sugar from the preserves ration.

If I am in order, I should like to address a question to the minister in connection with the statement he has just made. It is represented to me from my constituency, which is a substantial producer of maple sugar products, that the rationing has had the effect of reducing production because people are not willing to give up their sugar coupons for maple sugar. I should like to have that situation investigated. I may say that I took it up with the wartime prices and trade board and they tried to laugh me out of court, but I cannot be laughed out of court so easily.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, March 23, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to His Majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war- Mr. Ilsely-Mr. Bradette in the chair.

At the sitting of yesterday the member for York West referred to tungsten. I would like to ask the minister a few questions for the purpose of general information on the subject. I do not expect the replies to-day but I hope' he will note the questions and bring down the answers at his convenience. Tungsten has been a mineral of very great importance, particularly in the early part of 1942, so much so that there was general publicity in all mining papers as well as in all newspapers advising prospectors and miners to be on the lookout for scheelite ore from which tungsten is taken.
I speak on this matter for the reason that the Emerald mine in my district was looked upon as one of the most promising tungsten properties in the dominion. The owner was a resident of the United States. Negotiations for the purchase of this mine were entered into, with the result that the owner asked the government $1,750,000. I suppose that was what one might call wet weight, because the government expropriated the property and took it over at dry weight of $424,000 payable in United States funds. That is quite a difference.
The metals reserve corporation apparently proceeded to develop the property, although the property is in the name of the government. That property produced 132 tons of high-grade tungsten and 267 tons of low-grade tungsten concentrates.
I wanted to ask the minister first of all: Does the property remain in the name of the Canadian government? Has it been fully paid for, and in view of the fact that the mine has closed, that operations have ceased, that there is no more demand for tungsten, will the minister first note the question as to why this lack of need for tungsten has come about in such a short time? Was there not sufficient research work to determine whether there would be an oversupply in the United States, or was there not sufficient research work to tell whether there would be any specific amount required in Canada? I ask this because the advertisements in the public press encouraged

everybody to go after scheelite ore. I asked what expenditures had been made on the Emerald mine, and1 the reply was $829,000 for development. I took it for granted that $424,000 would be added to that for the expropriation of the mine. I wish to ask the minister if the $829,000 includes the cost of erecting the mill, because the development of the mine could not be proceeded with unless there was a mill. It is a very up-to-date mill.
We now have $829,000 and $424,000 of United States funds in the property while 267 tons of low grade concentrates, which yielded $70,000, have been shipped out. There are 132 tons of high grade concentrates left. What is the assay of the high grade concentrates? What will be the approximate value of them? What is the government going to do with these high grade concentrates, and what is the government going to do with the high grade concentrates from the various mines across the country which have been producing tungsten? They all went to considerable expense to get production under way.
In September last all operations at this Emerald mine ceased and the mill closed in October. Can the government not arrange to use that mill as a customs mill for prospectors of lead and zinc ores in the West Kootenay district? It may be necessary to have some alterations made, but as development cost $829,000 and the property $424,000, plus the cost of the mill, which is unknown, it represents a very large investment.
I should like to turn to the matter of publicity and the encouraging of prospectors to make a thorough search for the then much-needed tungsten, which to-day is' not needed at all. Is that situation brought about because the production in the United States is so greatj or the price of mining so much less. I wish to cite to the minister the case of a local prospector. A letter in reference to that case went to the Department of Mines four or five days ago, to which there has been no reply. I stress the Department of Mines because all the newspaper publicity urged prospectors to be on the lookout for scheelite and to send their samples to the Department of Mines. They were told if they did that they would get full information not only as to procedure but as to the names of the firms in the United States to which the tungsten concentrates could be shipped. I cite this case purely as a matter of justice in view of the publicity given.
This man was employed during the day. He had a property on which he thought there were scheelite indications. At his own expense he bought a mineral lamp and proceeded to mine his scheelite ore with the result
1S05

War Appropriation-Supplies
that he took out four tons of concentrates containing tungsten. He sent samples to the Department of Mines at Victoria. Apparently the provincial government and the federal government were acting in unison; however, most of his correspondence had been with the Department of Mines at Ottawa. As I say, he sent his samples to Victoria. He had them assayed and sent to the Minister of Mines. Apparently he did not get very much general information from Ottawa, but he directed another letter to the Minister of Mines in January, after information was received that there was no use for tungsten in Canada; that the Emerald mine had closed along with the mill. He asked the Minister of Mines where he could ship his concentrates. He had been told in those printed advertisements and publications from the Department of Mines-I suppose it applied to the federal and provincial departments-that when a man had tungsten concentrates which reached a specific assay the department would advise him to what firm in the United States to ship them, and he would be paid fifty per cent cash and the balance upon receipt of the concentrates and an assay by the United States firm to which they had been shipped. However, the Department of Mines told him there was no longer any use for concentrates. After the first of January he wrote to the Minister of Mines and asked whether it was worth while to proceed with the purchase of additional mining equipment in order that he might locate the main body of ore on his property. The Minister of Mines replied that a tungsten property is always of great value but at the present time there is no place to ship the concentrates.
Visualize a man putting in an eight hour shift and responding to the plea of the government to hunt for scheelite to produce tungsten concentrates. He puts in an eight hour shift at his everyday work. He was employed in the smelter. He wrote to the management of the mill of the Emerald mine, which is not over thirty or forty miles away, and the mill manager replied that he was unable to mill his Concentrates unless he could secure the permission of the Minister of Mines. He must have meant the federal Minister of Mines, because the property belongs to the federal government. Before he could get a reply the mill had closed. He then proceeded to break up the four tons of ore himself. It is a very hard job to break up four tons of ore. He put in his time in the evenings and on Sundays, and, as I said, he got out the high grade concentrates and the low grade concentrates. He did not ask the government to accept the low grade concentrates, but he wanted to get some reimbursement for his high grade concentrates. Unfortunately there
is no place to which he can ship. My contention, my plea and my suggestion is that it is only a matter of justice for the government to take that man's two tons of concentrates and pay him for them. They undertook to pay him fifty per cent cash as soon as he got an assay, the balance to be paid upon analysis by the firm to whom it was shipped. It is only a matter of justice that that prospector, who has gone the whole way, done everything that the government asked him to do, should be repaid for his effort or a market found for his concentrates. They have a million and a half in this Emerald property, and the government would not know what to do with it to-day any more than they would know how to fly. Why could they not compensate that prospector for two tons of concentrates?
I want to come now to the Kootenay-Florence mine, which is on Kootenay lake, and belongs to a Canadian firm. The metals reserve corporation, through the metals control board, entered into an agreement with that company. I want to ask the minister the terms under which that property is being operated. I know the owners are receiving a royalty, but I want to know also the price they receive per ton for the lead and zinc concentrates being shipped to the United States. My main purpose, however, is to ask the minister if he will not make use of that mill. It is a lead and zinc mill. The Emerald mill is a tungsten mill which could be altered to accommodate lead and zinc concentrates, but the Florence mill is being operated already. I ask the minister if arrangements cannot be made for the use of the Florence mill by local mines. There must be a customs mill in the West Kootenay district; otherwise you will discourage, as you have been discouraging, the production and shipment of lead and zinc, which is urgently required.
What did the Consolidated Mining and Smelting company do? They entered into an agreement with the British government to sell all their lead and zinc during the period of the war, and they are receiving 3-6 cents per pound for zinc. To-day the quotation in St. Louis for lead is 6-35 cents and for zinc 8-25 cents. I mention these quotations particularly because I want to appeal to hon. members to my left, who never seem to have a kindly word for the Consolidated Mining and Smelting company, which they look upon as a corporation which has no regard for industrial relations. I can assure them that the industrial relations of this company are not equalled by those of any other concern in the Dominion of Canada. Further I want to say to hon. members to my left that by
War Appropriation-Supplies

selling to the British government for about 3-6 cents per pound instead of at the prices quoted in the United States, which prices are received by any producers who ship their concentrates to the United States, this company has saved the British government about $22,000,000 annually ever since the outbreak of the war. I would ask my hon. friends to have a generous thought for one company which does not seem to operate purely for the exploitation of the country.

I shall be very glad at the next sitting to answer the questions which have been asked by the hon. member for Kootenay West.
While I am on my feet I should like to refer, to two matters which were discussed last evening. The first was in connection with the ownership of Clark Ruse Aircraft Limited. The reason I mention this is that certain statements made in the house last evening were quoted in the press to-day. The directors of the company are: J. Clark Ruse, president; Ewart Angus, vice-president; Mel Angus, secretary-; Harold Jeffries; Hon. J. Earl Lawson.
The directors, with the single exception of the estate of Alfred R. Caldwell, are all the shareholders and own the total share capital. The estate of Alfred R. Caldwell is represented by Hon. J. Earl Lawson, who is the solicitor for the company; and it was through Mr. Lawson that the capital invested in the company was raised. I suggest that the hon. member for York-Sunbury might be a little careful in talking unjustly about the officers of my department.
I did not make any attack; what I asked-
You did not ask; you stated.

Just a moment; the minister has referred to me and I am rising to a question of privilege. I asked whether the capital investment in the plant was to be a loss to the country, or how it was to be treated.
You made a statement.
Perhaps the minister misunderstood the purport of my question.
There was no question. You made a statement about a member of my department which you asked to have expunged from Hansard, and I agreed to have it expunged.
I never asked to have it expunged. Someone else asked to have it expunged, and I agreed to it, if you want the bald truth.
Not myself.

Not myself, either. I did not ask for it, but I agreed to it. The minister is on the wrong track. I was asking about the capital expenditure in the plant at Dartmouth, and now that operations there are -being reduced I wanted to know if that was to be a capital loss to the country, or what use it was to be put to. I said nothing about the ownership of the company. The minister has sought to bring that in, and I welcome the information but I did not ask for it.
You certainly made a statement about it, and I was answering that statement which, had it been true, would have caused a very serious situation in the department and in the country.
I will look it up in Hansard.

You will not find it in
Hansard, but you can find it in the typewritten sheets from which it was expunged.
I understood you agreed to have that done, and I agreed to it.
Nevertheless it appeared in the press, and I thought it deserved an answer.
I did not put it in the press, and I am not responsible for what was there.
You are responsible for what you say in the house, I think.
That is right, and I take full responsibility for it.

I understand it is the intention to go along with the estimates of the Minister of Munitions and Supply, as we did with those of the army, the navy and the air force. While the estimates set out specifically items covering almost everything one could discuss, there are some observations of a general nature I should like to make.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) stated in a general way the opinions held by this group respecting the minister's report to the committee. My own opinion is that under difficult conditions the minister has done an excellent job, from the inception of his department. When one stops to examine the record back to the outbreak of war, and realizes the position in which the minister was placed in a country totally unprepared for war, with the responsibility thrown into the minister's lap of putting Canada on a war-time basis, he can see that this was a big order to hand to any one man. The surprising feature is the success he has had, particularly in view of the lack of cooperation from the beginning on the part of those who were in a position to give him perhaps the only available assistance
180S
War Appropriation-Supplies

at that time. I refer to those organizations to which he handed so much power, a procedure for which I believe he has been justifiably criticized. When he first approached those organizations and asked for their cooperation in putting Canada on a war-time basis industrially, we remember that their only gesture of cooperation was that unless the clause providing for a limitation of profits to five per cent were removed, they would not be prepared to produce war materials.
The point I make is this: in examining the record of the Department of Munitions and Supply one must remember that the only machinery the department had to work with at that time was the then existing industrial establishment of the country. Any man who took that industrial machine and built from it the organization we now have must be handed a compliment, and it is one which I think he has justly earned. He had a terrific job, and received very little cooperation in the first instance from those who were in a position to give him real assistance.
The scene has changed, however, and a real organization has been built up. I agree with many hon. members who have said that to-day too much power rests in the hands of that group who are concerned about profits only. We do not quarrel with the controls, but rather with those who control, and what they control for. If the only desire in their minds is profits for themselves, that is a motive which the Canadian people, and particularly the members of this house, will have to watch very closely.
With respect to the industrial war machine that has been built up, the minister I think has proven that we have reached the peak of war production. The emphasis is changing; there is a slackening off, and a tendency on the part of those who are dominant in these controls, men from the larger industries, to create the opinion in the minds of the public generally that the war is near its end, and that the huge organization that has been built up for the purpose of prosecuting the war can now be unscrambled. I notice that many of the key people are resigning the positions which they have occupied for the past two years in the controls and are going back to their own private companies. When I say "going back", I should add that they are going back in name only, because they have never really left their own concerns. I think they reason this way: Controls have been developed, and certain legislation and orders in council have been passed, which make it unnecessary for us to remain in these controls any longer, because under the existing legislation and orders in council there is practically a guarantee to us that the emergency machine 
that was built up for war purposes will not be utilized in the aftermath of the war in competition with those of us who believe in private enterprise-whatever private enterprise may mean. I have lived under so-called private enterprise for forty-five years or so, and it has been so private, so mysterious, that most of the citizens of this country have not yet had an introduction to it. I could not give a definition of it; it is something really mysterious to me. But if by private enterprise they mean the concentration of wealth and power in the hands of a few men like Sir Herbert Holt and the Royal bank, I can understand that.
He is dead.	,

But he left footprints on the sands of time. If that is to be the motive in the future with respect to the utilization of this industrial war machine that has been built up, the Canadian people are in for a very unhappy experience.
I said a few nights ago that I consider the war supplies allocation board and the War Assets Corporation which have been set up under the Department of Munitions and Supply perhaps the most important post-war organizations that have been, instituted by the government. I have served on the reconstruction committee for the past two and a half years. The committee has heard many briefs and recommendations with regard to planning for the post-war period and creating jobs for those in the armed services when they return. But the only jobs that you will have in the post-war period which did not exist in 1939, when there were one million and a half people on relief in this country- and to-day many of those boys are in Sicily or Italy-will be the jobs created by this industrial war machine that has been built up under the Department of Munitions and Supply. But if that organization is not used for that purpose; if these industries are not converted to peace-time needs, you are not going to have any jobs for our boys to come back to from overseas. We have placed in the hands of the war supplies allocation board and the War Assets Corporation the power of utilizing, in such a way as they see fit, the great industrial organization that has been built up by the taxpayers of this country and from the very slight experience we have had with it so far I am sceptical as to how that power is going to be used. For instance, here is a statement in Toronto Saturday Night of a few weeks ago, "Canada far ahead on disposal of surplus war supplies." The thing that gives me concern in this article is that the manufacturers' association emphatically state that

War Appropriation-Supplies
in their opinion industry which has been created for war purposes must under no circumstances when the war ends be given to newcomers in the industrial set-up, to be used on a competitive basis with industries now in existence. In effect that means to me that those who dominated the industrial set-up in the field of private enterprise in 1939 before the war are of the opinion that this whole war machine should be scrapped now, that under no circumstances should the industrial organisation that has been built up during the War be used for the purpose of creating peace-time necessities and come into competition with the existing industrial organizations. That is the opinion of your manufacturers' association and your chamber of commerce; there is no doubt about that. The chamber of commerce in making their presentation to the reconstruction committee not so long ago stated emphatically that one of the basic principles they were advocating was that immediately on the cessation of hostilities the whole industrial machine that had been built up during the war must be scrapped and the field left open to private enterprise. The point I wish to make there is this, and I have no ulterior motive at all; I do not care what kind of tag you hang on to your order of society, but unless that order of society takes care of the needs of the people it has no right to exist.
We are all agreed on that.

Then we must be in disagreement with the manufacturers' association and the chamber of commerce who advocate a return to 1939 conditions in the field of industry in Canada. That is their policy, and it is one with which I and those of us in this group disagree. I am glad to hear the hon. member for Rosedale say that we are all agreed on the principle of establishing an order of society that will take care of the needs of the people regardless of any particular group that may be injured in the process.
In the matter of utilizing the existing wartime industrial organization, I have had one or two little experiences which indicate to me that those who have the authority to dispose of surplus war materials and supplies have a certain definite policy that they are going to follow. Let me give the minister one example, a very small one perhaps.
An ex-service man who had been overseas for a couple of years came back and took work at a shipyard. He had previously been a miner. When the emergency fuel order came out he was directed by national selective service to go back to his old employment as a miner. He did so, going to the section to 100-114
which he was allocated by the selective service. His family was in another part of the country, and he desired to move them so that they could be together, but he could not find a place to live. There are barracks located in that town comprising some forty buildings. The barracks are new. They had been used for a short time, but were then unoccupied. He suggested to me that I get in touch with national defence with a view to his buying one of these buildings and convert it into a dwelling for himself and his family. I wrote several departments, not knowing exactly who or what this war allocations committee or corporation was. I was advised, after some considerable delay that, as far as selling any of these buildings was concerned, by virtue of the buildings having been put on land owned or leased by Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation Limited, that company had first option on them and it was believed that they would utilize them as homes for miners who might be directed from other industries into that section. Nothing has been done in that matter so far. The ex-service man who was directed to come back to that particular occupation still lives apart from his family.
I tried again. One of the larger credit unions in that area, desirous of obtaining more office space, wanted to purchase one of the. buildings. Upon writing about the matter I received exactly the same information.
These are small illustrations of a point which I wish to leave with the minister. My conception of the principle upon which this corporation and committee are going to work is this. Much of the money which through the minister's department has been put into industry for the purpose of expanding existing industry and developing new production has gone into plant and equipment on land held by private companies. Presumably the decision rendered by the board in the case I have mentioned is that upon which the whole industrial machine built by the minister's department will be disposed of.
I did not just follow the hon. member. May I ask, did he get his information from the disposal board in the case of the barracks at New Glasgow?
The barracks were at Glace Bay, Nova Scotia.
Well, did he get his information from the army or the disposal board? Who told him?

In the one case, national
defence secured it through the 'board; in the second case I myself secured it through the board.

Through the disposal board?

Through the allocation committee.

Ordinarily land acquired by
the army for barracks purposes has been .purchased by the army. I am not familiar with the arrangements. But as to buildings paid for by the Department of Munitions and Supply, in practically all cases the land is owned in fee by the crown.

I cited those two cases
merely to indicate the opinion I had formed because of this particular incident. Several orders in council I have seen appear to bear that out. For instance, you have investments in the plants of Canada Car and Foundry and Dominion Steel and Coal. Plants have been created, and when the war is over they will no longer be needed for war purposes and the committee 'has the right to tear the .plant down or move it somewhere else. But if it is not removed it reverts to the company on whose property it was built. I am. not blaming the minister for this. As I said at the opening of my remarks, he was faced with the responsibility of having to organize an industrial machine and had to use everybody and everything that he could use, and he did under those circumstances exactly as I would have done, or anyone else would have done; he built the machine without quibbling over details or technicalities. But that period is past. The time has now arrived when the minister, the members of this house, and everyone who is interested in ensuring the maintenance of full employment after the war, should see to it that legislation is enacted which will protect the investments the Canadian people have in our industrial set-up, so that they may be utilized when the war is over to do the job that everyone here agrees should be done, namely, provide employment for every last man and woman who is in the services and for those in war industries who have made it possible for the allied nations to put on an offensive to-day in Europe.
There is another matter I should like to bring to the minister's attention. I may have a little difficulty in proving to the chairman that it belongs exactly here; I think it does, but I am- giving him fair warning. First, however, I want to compliment the hon. member for Caribou (Mr. Turgeon). He pretty much agrees with what I have said, for according to a report in one of the Toronto newspapers he stated in a speech he made in that city that "free enterprise may not survive the end of the war." I am very glad to hear that statement from the chairman of the reconstruction committee. I have worked with him cm that committee, and I find him very broad* minded and farsighted.

afraid of.

He sees the handwriting on
the wall.

I have read it. It is a very good statement. He visualizes the utilization of the war machine in the aftermath of the war pretty much as I have tried to describe it this afternoon?

The other matter I should like to bring to the minister's attention is one on which we may not see eye to eye. A few months ago the Prime Minister tabled in this chamber an order declaring a national emergency in fuel. After having that particular branch of our industry in many hands in the past several years, he centred the emergency organization of the fuel industry in the Department of Munitions and Supply. Of course Munitions and Supply was merely delegated authority under that order to get an increased production in fuel, necessary to the war effort. That organization has not worked out as well as I should have liked. Fortunately this winter has been very mild, and as a result we managed to get through without any great difficulty.
I notice according to the press and from consultations with union officials from Nova Scotia that in both the coal sections of Canada to-day there is considerable unrest in the mining industry. In the Alberta field, as pointed out by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston), there is actual unemployment, because of some faulty fuel policy in that particular area. In Nova Scotia there is a different situation. Their fears are for the future. But what I want to impress on the mind of the minister is that from both sections of Canada to-day come proposals, from operators and from miners' unions, to meet in Ottawa with government officials for the purpose of deciding on a national fuel policy. The operators in this country are not in a position to decide from day to day where they are going.
The markets are very uncertain, and as I see it in Nova Scotia, if the war were to terminate to-morrow, with the market arrangement that exists at the present time you would not have markets to guarantee a two days a week operation in the mining industry in that

War Appropriation-Supplies
province. I am not going to say what the situation is in Alberta, because I do not know, but our people in Nova Scotia are very much concerned about it. There are many angles to the problem, but I will not go into all of them.	,
One thing in the emergency arrangement that I think is unjust is that in Alberta, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, in the matter of domestic fuel, because of the increase in wages to the miners a substantial increase in the price of domestic fuel was permitted by the government. In other words, the consuming public of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Alberta and Saskatchewan have had to pay for the increases in wages given the miners in those provinces. On the other hand, the consuming public in central Canada, Quebec and Ontario, are in the reverse position. When you had to supply the domestic market in those two provinces, the small tariff that was against American coal was removed, something like 50 cents a ton-35 cents on some and 50 cents on others. In addition, importers of coal in central Canada were subsidized in order to hold the price ceiling. So that taxpayers generally across Canada are maintaining the price ceiling and absorbing the increased cost in domestic fuel in the two central provinces. While in the eastern and western provinces there has been some increase in the wages of those who dig the coal, the consuming public in those provinces have had to take on an additional burden in the way of an increased cost of domestic coal. Therefore, they are paying for the maintenance of the price ceiling in Ontario through taxation, and they are paying for the fact that there were increased wages in that industry, both east and west, when the government permitted a slight upward revision.
I should correct my hon. friend. There is no bonus on coal imported into the central provinces-that is, on steam coal. Thera may be a small bonus on anthracite, but there is no bonus on steam coal.
I agree with the minister. I was speaking of domestic fuel. It is anthracite that is mostly used in the central provinces for domestic purposes, but my whole argument is based on domestic fuel.
You use anthracite in the maritime provinces, and it is bonused. You were talking of steam coal in the maritimes and domestic in the western provinces.

We use very little anthracite in the maritime provinces, and American coal imported for metallurgical purposes is bonused 100-1141
to a certain extent. There is a drawback of 35 cents a ton. All coal used for metallurgical purposes is subject to that provision. It is a long story which I will not go into.' But both east and west the domestic consumer of fuel has a legitimate grievance in that he is contributing to the whole national set-up in the maintenance of the price ceiling as it exists in the two central provinces; and in addition he has a direct levy because of the increase given the miners in those provinces. It is something that should receive the consideration of those who are responsible for the fuel policy.
The other angle is this. In the house on several occasions I have suggested that in the field of fuel Canada definitely lacks a policy. There is no doubt about that, and for the past twenty years there has been enough money spent in delegations, in briefs, and in royal commissions to reorganize the whole industry. As I pointed out a moment ago, the fear in Nova Scotia is that we are facing a repetition of what happened in the last war. In the last war we lost the Quebec market completely, and that is the only economic market for Nova Scotia coal in Canada. United States coal to-day is going clear through to Riviere du Loup. That market has been completely handed over to the United States operators.
In the reconstruction committee when this subject was under consideration I specifically questioned those who represented both the companies and the fuel board. I asked if they were taking care this time, when handing over markets for emergency purposes, not to repeat the mistake of 1917 and 1918 and give away those markets without any understanding or agreement safeguarding the Canadian taxpayers against repurchase over a period of years at a cost of millions of dollars, as actually happened after the last war. I was informed then by the representatives of the fuel board that, as far as markets were concerned, there was no agreement or understanding and that it was a matter of getting that coal in during the emergency as quickly as possible without any regard to what was going to happen in the future.
In view of the fact that the miners themselves, their unions and the provincial governments are taking the initiative at this time in trying to head off something that may be very serious, should the war end within the next year or two, the minister should now inaugurate some kind of organization in Ottawa, or give instructions to those, under his charge, operating in that field, to see to it that this delegation is received and that a definite policy is mapped out for the Canadian industry in order to avoid what I can see
War Appropriation-Supplies

coming, in Nova Scotia at any rate, immediately on the cessation of hostilities if the situation remains as it is at the present time.
The industry in Nova Scotia requires a complete overhauling. Some people say, you cannot compete with American industries because they are mechanized and electrified. That is true. I can tell the minister that the industry in Nova Scotia is as fully mechanized as it can be. The mines there are old, and they cannot be further mechanized; and what is more, you cannot electrify them. You cannot put in . electric cutting and loading machines because the mines are submarine and very gaseous. Someone'said to me, "You fellows fought mechanization a few years ago", and I replied, "Yes, we did in one colliery, one of the most gaseous on the north American continent." It was new, with a very gaseous seam of coal, and if you installed an electric cutting ana loading machine, throwing sparks four hundred yards, you would blow the cover off the mine in a short time. We were right in fighting it. It cannot be done in those old mines, and that is something that must be considered.
The minister is an engineer, and I think he has a fair conception of the sort of problem with which we are faced. I should like to see that department, now that it is responsible in that field, institute an examination of that whole industry in Nova Scotia from the operating standpoint. I know there is one man in the fuel set-up, Mr. Frank Neate, secretary of the fuel control board, who has a thorough knowledge of the industry. I believe that if he were permitted to sit in with a miner's committee and the operators who are desirous of framing some kind of workable fuel policy for Canada, he has both the technical and the practical knowledge to do a really good job. I believe he could map out something that would be workable. It is a post-war problem which means a lot to Nova Scotia. The whole economy of that province is based on the coal industry, which at this time requires a thorough and solid examination.- Something has been done; I do not know whether it was through the minister's department or not. Substantial increases in wages were given the miners of that province, and for the first time in the history of that industry in Canada a week's vacation with pay was granted in the last agreement. That was something the miners used to dream about, but they never imagined it would happen.
Without going into all the ramifications and technicalities and the many things that one could talk about hour after hour I want to emphasize the necessity of examining that industry in Nova Scotia with the end in view

of reorganizing and stabilizing it. I could tell the minister a long story about the machinery he set up to go down there to get emergency production and all that kind of thing. You cannot get production in offices. You cannot sit in Moncton and imagine that the industry is going to be improved. It is a job that has to be done where the coal is produced. It was not done in that way. Divine Providence was kind to the minister this winter in helping him out in the coal situation; otherwise I think he would have have had more headaches. I should like seriously to advise him to do something about examining the whole set-up of that industry for the future.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) has given us quite a comprehensive picture of the tremendous production achieved by war plants during the last year and even since the beginning of the war. He has, moreover, outlined the programme he proposes to carry out during the current year , and he requests us to vote considerable amounts for those purposes. But if such a result has been achieved, it was through the cooperation of the worker who is an essential element of production, and it is imperative that he should be treated with fairness. Unfortunately, according to some statements I have received, in certain industries under government control, and especially at the nitro munition plant operated by the Defence Industries on Salaberry island, at Valleyfield, and at the Bouchard plant, near Saint Therese, the workers are victims of glaring injustice.
On March 9 last, I gave notice of a certain number of questions relating to the laying-off of some employees in those industries, that is to say, at the Bouchard plant or at the nitro plant on, Salaberry island, Valleyfield, and to the replacement of those workers by people from other provinces and particularly from Nobel, in the province of Ontario. I had hoped that I could obtain answers to those questions before making my present reWrks. Unfortunately I fear that the debate may come to an end before my questions are answered. Besides, the bon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Bertrand) following some newspaper comments, has referred this -week to such cases of injustice which I mean to bring before the committee. As a matter of fact, employees with a long record of service, men who have worked in those plants for one, two and three years are laid off and replaced by men from other provinces and especially from the Nobel plant which- has been closed. Such is the glaring injustice done to those men. They have lived in the locality for many years as

War Appropriation-Supplies
permanent residents, they own their homes, and1 have families to support; they have worked almost since the beginning at the nitro plant in Valleyfield, and to-day they are laid off and replaced by people from other provinces. That is an intolerable injustice against which I must strongly protest. It cannot be claimed that those men are not competent because the fact that they were kept for two and even three years shows that they were considered as efficient, but to-day they are dismissed. Sometimes, another procedure is followed; the man is called and offered a lower position, with a greatly reduced salary, so that he is placed in the alternative of leaving or remaining at a lower salary with which, he cannot support his family. That is a devious means of dismissing him to make room for others. I admit that production has decreased, but if so, why does the management hire men from other provinces, such as those who have come from the Nobel plant? If there has been a reduction in the number of workers needed, why are outsiders hired? That is a lame excuse.
The government have some responsibility in that respect because those industries are under their control, inasmuch as the government have themselves established institutions such as the Allied1 War Supplies, which later on have entrusted to other companies the operation of some plants. But those institutions, organizations, or companies have been established with the taxpayer's money and this afternoon the Minister of Munitions and Supply has told us how much the government had to pay for the Nitro plant, on Salaberry island, at Valleyfield. Consequently, the taxpayers, the workers from whose weekly salary a deduction is made for war taxes, are entitled to some consideration and they have, in preference to others, a right to earn their living in the locality where they have always lived.
May I point out one case. The other day I received from a worker a letter in which he said: "I have two sons in the air force; one of them has recently been repatriated on account of illness; two other sons of mine have just been called for training in the army. 1 have a family to support and I have been laid off. How was it done? I have been offered a greatly reduced salary with which I could not support my family."
Those are facts which I wanted to bring to the attention of the committee, and particularly of the Minister of Munitions and Supply.
There is another fact which I also wish to emphasize. Ever since the plant on Salaberry island has begun its operations, local workers have been treated like neglected members of the family. All main positions have
been given to outsiders, and the positions left for local workers have always been minor ones. Let no one claim that competent men could not be found. I could mention particular cases, but I do not want to name any one, not because an injustice might be done but because the workers might thereby suffer unpleasant consequences. I know that, in some cases, a man in a minor position has had to teach a man of higher rank how the work was to be done, the salary of that lower man being much smaller and the man who outranked him having been brought from .outside to be placed above him.
I hope the Minister of Munitions and Supply will give careful consideration to the few remarks I made not only in the interest of the working class but also in the interest of peace in the post-war period. We hear a great deal about the post-war era, but if we really want to prepare it and avoid perhaps a number of calamities and a certain amount of ill feeling, we must give fair treatment to all citizens., and the working man should be- included among them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
I have just stated that Allied War Supplies Limited is connected with the government. This firm controls the operation of explosives factories, and so forth. However, Defence Industries Limited and Canadian Industries Limited are private enterprises. It seems to me that these private firms are entitled to hire anyone they wish.
While on this subject, the hon. member will perhaps allow me to refer to a news sheet which he will recognize, no doubt. It is entitled Le Bloc. I believe it to be the organ of the party of which the hon. member is the leader. In its March 15 issue, this news sheet contains a number of inaccuracies, not to say
IMr. Chevrier.]
numerous falsehoods. I have just stated the first one. It starts by asserting that Defence Industries Limited is a crown company. It follows on with a claim that the workers of the Bouchard plant, at Ste. Therese, have often been discriminated against. I have here a report from the president of Allied War Supplies stating that no worker from the province of Ontario has been hired by or transferred to the Bouchard plant. The news sheet Le Bloc claims further that these persons have all had their expenses paid by the government. This report has it that in no case the expenses connected with transferring and hiring the men have been borne by Allied War Supplies Limited but that, on the contrary, the workers themselves have always paid their own expenses.
To conclude, I wish to point out to the hon. member that 1,665 citizens of Quebec have gone to work in war factories of the province of Ontario. Three or four hundred of them are located in Sarnia, a considerable number have secured jobs in Kingston, others in the Niagara peninsula, and others still in Kitchener. The hon. member may perhaps allow me to mention a report, just handed to me, published in a Kitchener newspaper of March 21, 1944. It is, therefore, of very recent date. The report points out that 300 Canadians from the province of Quebec have reached that town seeking employment in war factories, but could not secure living accommodation. Nevertheless, the mayor of the town issued a public statement requesting his fellow citizens to welcome them, to find accommodation, whether rooms or lodgings, for them and the local people have responded to his appeal. I fail to see why my hon. friend has brought this matter up, for it must not be forgotten that if, at times, our people seem to be discriminated against, there are, on the other hand, in the province of Ontario, a large number of them who secure employment in similar circumstances. From the newspaper report I was referring to a while ago, I shall now quote the words of Mayor Meinzinger of Kitchener:	'	.
Kitchener is fortunate in having to receive some 300 French Canadians which are come to this place to help relieve the labour shortage in local plants. We all appreciate the seriousness of the war, and therefore must feel that it is the duty of each and every one to assist in the problem. I appeal to every home-owner and property-owner in Kitchener, Waterloo, Centreville and Bridgeport, and other centres in which we have bus and street car facilities, to open their homes to these men.
In short, room was made to accommodate these workers. As I said before, a good number of them had come to Ontario and I cannot believe the hon. member for Beauharnois-

(Translation): Mr. Chairman I intervene in the discussion, but this does not mean that I no longer have for my hon. successor in the county of Laprairie, the genial member for Beauhamois-Laprairie (Mr. Raymond) all the sympathy deserved by a member who rises above the petty jibes of politics to deal with a matter of public interest. The distinguished parliamentary assistant to the hon. the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Chevrier), has replied to the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie and I might say that his replies have relieved my conscience to some extent. If it were true that, as stated by the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie, citizens of the constituency of Beauharnois-Laprairie and of the county of Terrebonne had been dismissed and replaced by outsiders, regardless of my political allegiance, I would join with the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie in protesting against such a discrimination. And I am sure that the hon. the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) and the hon. member for Stormont would support us, as no one wishes to commit an injustice. However the hon. member for Stormont declared, on the strength of written information in his possession, that no citizen of Ontario went to Beauharnois or to the Bouchard plant . . .

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: No worker.

... to take the place of persons who had been dismissed. In my opinion, the matter is settled to the satisfaction of the committee. But while I was listening to my hon. friend from Beauharnois-Laprairie defending as always the rights of the working man, my thoughts dwelt upon the general policy of the party which he has deemed advisable to create. To give a rather
mild explanation of the policy of my hon. friend, I might say that if his party's policy is not one of non-participation it is at least one of limited nationalism-I would not call it extreme nationalism, as this would be too strong a term. On the basis of this policy, my hon. friend and all those who honour him with their confidence, find that we have no justification for taking part in the war; they claim that England has treated the French-Canadians unfairly and for this reason has forfeited any right to our sympathy ; they hold that all that we have accomplished since the outbreak of the war has involved useless expenditures of money and wholly unjustified sacrifices of human lives. Is this not, Mr. Chairman, the attitude of my hon. friend from Beauharnois-Laprairie?
In my student days, I had the opportunity of attending a meeting in Montreal where Sir Wilfrid Laurier was to speak in favour of voluntary enlistment. At this point, I shall indulge in a digression to tell my hon. friends of the Bloc Populaire they are mistaken when they claim that they have always been opposed to war. The hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie was himself a Liberal in those days and I, though quite young at the time, followed the example set by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and favoured participation in the war of 1918 though, like the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie, I objected to conscription.
I never favoured participation in the war, neither in 1914 nor at the present time.
If my hon. friend states he was then opposed to participation, it does not speak well for him since he was as mute as a fish.
That is of no consequence. You want to credit me with opinions I never held.

My hon. friend asserts he was not in favour of participation in war and he admits not having said a word about it at that time. Truth did not come to him in a flash or in some sort of vagary and he did not suddenly decide to declare himself opposed to participation in war.
I was not in politics.

The hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie only minimizes his own merit and intellect when he claims he was not interested in politics. No intelligent man ever takes that attitude.
Mr. Chairman, let us get back to our onions, -I beg your pardon, I mean the Bloc Populaire. This party, and I speak without a trace
War Appropriation-Supplies

of sarcasm, stands against all participation and, above all, against the billion dollar gift. What nightmares this has given them! They have lost sleep over it. Just think, to sacrifice our sons is a great deal, to take part in the war is far too much, but to raise one billion dollars a year from Canada's public funds and give it to England, a wealthier country, is truly scandalous!
When I hear my hon. friend complain that the workers of Beauharnois-Laprairie or some other district of the province of Quebec are not treated fairly, I can't help thinking: What a paradox! In fact, my hon. friend is opposed to participation in the war, he objects to any grant that might help those who held the fort in England. When France, our former beloved motherland lay crushed in June 1940, and one country alone could repulse the enemy, the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie and his followers deemed that nothing should be done. The house of our next-door neighbour but one is burning down and the wind blows towards the home of the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie. He says to his children and his employees: "Never mind, I have a grudge against that fellow, let the fire destroy his property". But he is not far-sighted enough to think that before the house of his third neighbour has stopped burning, the flames will have reached the roof of his own house and it will then be too late to do anything. That thought has not occurred to him.
How inconsistent is the stand taken by my hon. friend! He claims that work should be given to those people, but how could they have had it had we not participated in this war, had we followed his advice and done nothing? Let my hon. friend rise in a few moments and tell us how many unemployed there would be in Valleyfield and everywhere in the country if we had done nothing.
Will the hon. member permit me to ask him a question?

I would ask my .ion, friend to let, me proceed with my remarks. I have not interrupted him.
Mr. Chairman, as far as I am concerned, while respecting the opinions of those who do not support my views, I find it strange that we should be considered as blind followers of a party which has betrayed the country and the French Canadians. For months and months, Mr. Chairman, ever since the outbreak of war, we have been charged with having betrayed our race. However, we have said nothing because what was most urgent, what had to be done regardless of any revile-ment, was to help England. Even those who

had no love for that country before the war, because of the prejudice that had been spread by so-called historians, even those who had no love for that country realized the situation. Like our leader, the Prime Minister of this country, we had at first hoped that because of the Maginot line, which gave us such great hopes before 1939, Canada's participation would only be moderate. But when all countries of the European continent had, one after the other-France, our former motherland being the last one to succumb-been overwhelmed by the enemy, who would have been stupid enough, for the petty satisfaction of saying that he had not changed his mind, to refuse to give all he had, to devote all his energy, his work and his efforts to help England? And when the outstanding man who now leads the government of England said, at a time when the whole European continent was under Hitler's heel: "We shall fight on the beaches and the landing grounds, in the fields, in the streets and on the hills. We shall never surrender," could we have abandoned to their fate such men, whom some of us, without any reason, do not like? Could we have refrained from going to their help? Only a lack of knowledge of our own history could have prompted us to do that. Every school boy has a sufficient knowledge of history to recall especially the Treaty of Paris, signed in 1763, after our former motherland had been defeated on the Plains of Abraham, in 1759, and in Europe in 1763.
What was the first of the peace conditions laid down by the victor? It was the cession of Canada to England. Anyone with a knowledge of history knows that history repeats itself and he realizes that if, in 1940, following the collapse of France, England had been overwhelmed, the first peace term would have been the surrender to Germany of all the rights of the British crown over Canadian territory. Is this what my hon. friend wanted? I know that it is not so. For our part, we did not remain idle; we did not imitate the ancient Greeks, as reported by the glorious history of Greece. While Phillip, by resorting to the same method as is being used to-day by Hitler, was trying by every available means to seize neighbouring countries, the Greeks who should have heeded the advice of Demosthenes who was urging them to prepare to defend themselves against the common enemy, remained complacent and formed "blocs" such as we have to-day. My hon. friend from Beauharnois-Laprairie knows what happened to Greece. She %vas subjugated by Phillip and invaded by his son, Alexander the Great.
But, thanks to the foresight and vision of our leaders and particularly of the Prime

War Appropriation-Supplies
Minister of Canada, we decided not to wait until England, the next country on Hitler's time-table after France, was brought to her knees. All the colonies, all the Dominions, all freedom-loving and democratic countries rallied one after another to England's assistance, and the rest is history. Thanks to the unanimous contribution of all freedom-loving peoples, we may now hope that before long, Hitler the tyrant-I trust I do not displease the hon. member for Beauharnois-Lhprairie in calling him so-Hitler the tyrant of modern times will have reached the end of his rope.
Mr. Chairman, at an appropriate moment, and with all good faith and sincerity, with malice towards none but with an understanding of truth as I see it, I wished to state why we, the Liberal party, in spite of the insults that have been and still will be heaped upon us, will continue to fight for democracy and will keep up the struggle until we have triumphed. The history of a later age will record that we protected not only those who understood the situation as we do, but also those who refused to see daylight, like our friends of the Bloc Populaire.

Last evening the minister said that there is no longer a shortage of material used in farm implements. This statement is at variance with the finding of the war expenditures committee which reported on January 26 of this year, after a thorough inquiry into the possibility of an immediate increase in the supply of farm implements. The committee stated that they had been assisted by farm implement companies; representatives of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture; Mr. Cruickshank, the metals coordinator; Mr. Bloom, administrator for agricultural implements; Mr. Hoey, associate steel controller of munitions and supply; Mr. Fowler, secretary to general counsel, wartime prices and trade board; Mr. Gavsie, assistant counsel, Department of Munitions and Supply.
May I ask my hon. friend on what date the evidence was taken?
I am not sure about that.
It makes quite a difference, because the situation has eased greatly in the last few months. I was speaking of the position to-day.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: It is over a year old, is it not?

No; some time in January.

I understand it is January of this year. The report is dated January 26, 1944. The finding is as follows:
Shortages which still exist and which will retard production of ample quantities of farm implements:
There is ample factory productive capacity in Canada to handle a much greater volume of implement production than we now have. The major problems now facing the industry are as follows:	(a) shortage of malleable
castings, due to volume of war production work;
(b)	shortage of ball and roller bearings;
(c)	shortage of seasoned fir and oak required for the production of certain types of farm machinery; (d) shortage of experienced manpower.
In 1939, at the time of the declaration of war, there were 53,000 tractors in Britain. In 1942 they had 150,000 tractors. The number of implements used in connection with these tractors has jumped from 200,000 in 1939 to well over a million in 1942.
In Canada, for 1944, production of essential farm machinery will be brought up to 80 per cent of the 1940-41 output, and spare parts to 150 per cent of that output. Under this control, only 10,000 of the 26,000 tractor orders can be filled during 1944. In Britain to-day, with less than one-third of the cultivated acreage of Canada, there are more tractors in use than we have available in Canada.
In more normal times, some years ago, farmers of western Canada spent approximately 850,000,000 annually upon farm implements. On account of depreciation and as a result of lessened purchasing power for a number of years prior to the outbreak of war in 1939, it was estimated at that time by implement manufacturers that it would require approximately 8200,000,000 to bring our farm implement equipment up to date.
Agriculture is an industry engaged in the production of foodstuffs, an industry with approximately 735,000 branch factories across Canada. Approximately 450,000 men and women have left the farms of Canada for service in the armed forces or in war industries.
The point I should like to make is that, with our farm labour shortages, tractors and especially combines along with other essential implements should be made available to as great an extent as is reasonably possible in order to assist in solving our labour problems.
The statement of the minister last evening, as I pointed out, is a contradiction of the report of the war expenditures committee in the past few weeks, and I trust that he will clarify this situation. I think he will realize that this is a very important matter and that our farmers need as soon as possible a much

War Appropriation-Supplies

greater output of farm implements, provided that it does not interfere with the production of essential equipment for the battlefield.
It was pointed out in a return brought down the other day that there have been issued from September 10, 1939, to March 15, 1944, 42,398 orders in council and 23,287 minutes of treasury board; that, since the present session of parliament commenced on January 28, 1944, to March 15, 1944, 1,186 orders in council and 850 minutes of treasury board have been passed. Therefore, I think, one may realize how difficult it is to follow all the various orders which are issued, not only orders in council but orders of these various controllers.
I should appreciate it if the minister could clarify this situation. The controllers in his department sat in with and gave evidence to the war expenditures committee. As a result we have their report, and for the sake of the producers from coast to coast the minister should make a statement to clear up this matter.

I should like to answer the hon. member immediately. I was reporting on the position in my own department as regards controls. In the years 1941, 1942 and the first eight or nine months of 1943 there was a very tight steel situation in this country; it was necessary to ration every use of steel outside of direct war use; but in that , period certain allocations of steel were made to the agricultural industry. The industry is administered by the wartime prices and trade board; nevertheless, since we control the use of war materials, the allocation in these years was made by agreement between the steel controller of my department and the agricultural implements administrator of the wartime prices and trade board.
During the last few months we have had sufficient steel for all reasonable purposes and the restrictions on use of steel in agricultural implements have been removed.
My hon. friend spoke of other situations. One was the supply of malleable castings. There is sufficient capacity, I think, for the manufacture of malleable castings in this country. The difficulty there is that malleable castings have in the past been largely imported into this country, owing to the fact that malleable castings made in large volume cost considerably less than the volume which was made in that time in Canada. The result is that the malleable castings business must be built up if it is immediately to take the whole load of the agricultural industry. However, we have that capacity in Canada, and the situation will be met as rapidly as the output can be built up.
[Mr. J. A. Ross.)
As regards ball bearings, of course we in Canada do not make ball bearings, and that is a situation which would not come within the jurisdiction of my department. That may be a bottle-neck, so far as I know; but there is no regulation of my department, at least-and when I speak of "my department", I refer to the administration of the controls of the raw material-which would interfere with the manufacture of implements.
Mr. FR'ASER (Peterborough West): What is the position with regard to metal roofing?

There is no immediate hope for the release of metal roofing. Productive capacity for the manufacture of thin sheet is very badly overloaded, and plants are working to capacity on uses of much higher priority than thin sheets for roofing, to which my hon. friend refers.
Metal roofing for barns.
There is no possibility of obtaining this for a few months yet.
Even for patching?
Yes, for patching there will be sufficient under certain conditions.

Last evening the hon. member for York-Sunbury made what I thought was a rather provoking criticism of the Minister of Munitions and Supply, wherein he alleged that there was geographical discrimination in the distributing of war industries across Canada. In that he was referring to the report on the government's financial expansion of the industrial capacity of Canada. I think the criticism of the hon. member was unfair, distorted and incorrect, and I will deal with one or two items to show how misleading it was and how unfairly it would present the matter to the house.
Does the hon. member think the maritimes are getting a square deal?

I will come to that. On page 1790 of Hansard the hon. member for York-Sunbury is reported as follows:
Then there is a table 1A-11, general purchasing and miscellaneous, purchases of merchandise. Crown plants government operated, nil; crown companies government operated, nil; crown plants operated by private corporations, $5,000; privately owned and operated plants, general merchandising; Trenton Steel Works is the only one and it received $23,268 out of a total of $530,972,648.
The hon member had exhausted his time and he was stopped by the Chairman at a very opportune place, because he skipped over part of the report. He left out the last pages

altogether; perhaps the reason was that he was obliged to sit down. In the last part of the report the majority of the items were for the maritime provinces. ... it is the whole table I am talking about. For the whole table that I am referring to, which covers a net expenditure of $83,462,508, the actual total expenditure in the maritimes was $2,022,671. That is the only one in the whole page. Coming then to machine guns and small arms-

You are too easily satisfied.
Mr. IvINLEY: I believe in the truth, and in keeping the record straight. He was presenting to the house a picture of war-time industry, conveying to the people what they were receiving in the war industrial endeavour of the nation. But this is only a very small part of the industrial endeavour of Canada. We have the estimates of the army, navy and the air force, and surely, in computing what goes to any section of the country in our war expenditures, we must include the whole picture; otherwise we get something which is dislocated and distorted.
The people of the maritimes know the picture.

He might have mentioned the great development in Shelburne, the great naval base there. He said nothing about the great naval training depot at Deep Brook. He said nothing about the development at Sydney or the developments at Halifax.

Sydney; was that the place where another dock fell into the harbour?	,

And all points east.

No, I am not.
No.

And I have not been for many years. But it does not lie in the mouths of the Progressive Conservative party to talk about development in the maritime provinces. The hon. gentleman has asked a question and I will answer it. The Liberal government once was in power in Nova Scotia for forty years.
Too Jong.

I admit it was too long, longer than a government in any other part of the British empire. They were dying of old age, and a friend of mine, who was also a friend of these gentlemen, the late Hon. on for another term when they were defeated, bringing back only a remnant of the men they elected when they went into power.
It is the industrial tariff and concentration of industry that has ruined Nova Scotia, the tariff that has built up big industries in central Canada. The idea of the men who created this situation in this country now coming to us in war time and saying, "You should have more in Nova Scotia because you have been neglected in years gone by," looks like a Daniel come to judgment. At the present time I believe that Nova Scotia has a degree of development which is better than we have had in many years. If we increase our development beyond the labour that we can supply to industry we should be creating a condition that is not good. At the present time labour is coming into Nova Scotia from other parts of Canada and I am greatly concerned about it because it is creating confusion. I wish to tell the Minister of Labour that we shall hold him to account if labour that has come in from other parts of the country continues to be employed and Nova Scotians are discharged.
Last night the Minister of Munitions and Supply told the hon. member for York South that when he took hold of that department it was his job to create an industrial machine to carry on the war, and in doing that he had to survey the situation and build where he could get the support naturally from those who could give it to him quickly. With the foundation of industrj' in Canada, as it was, centralized in the central provinces, they would get the major portion of the financial assistance to expand. We in the maritimes looked for that part of the development for which we were particularly suited and where we could do the job that was required at tidewater by men who serviced the sea activities.
There were plants in the smaller towns along the south coast of Nova Scotia which had survived since the last war. I know that during the last war one plant in Lunenburg had a trade all over this country and in foreign lands. They shipped equipment for ships to Greece, British Columbia, South America and the West Indies. When this war broke out, those plants were particularly suitable for marine work; and the minister, by providing new marine railway equipment, and by helping some of them that needed it to get the proper machinery, made a good move. This created a situation which has enabled Nova Scotia to make a contribution to the navy which has been so much praised in this

committee and which is a credit to the shipbuilders and the ship repair plants and personnel of Nova Scotia. .
My chief object for the future is to hold what we have in Nova Scotia. If we can hold what we have, and if we can keep employed the number of people that we have employed there, I shall be satisfied. That is much better than if we had, say a hundred thousand more men in Nova Scotia, because they of necessity must lose their jobs when the war is over.
That does not need to happen.
I think there will be some disillusionment.
So do I.
But I wish to tell my hon. friend that I do not think it will be as bad as it was in the last war because-
That is a matter of opinion.	.

This time labour is earning more money. More money is being distributed among the people. There is a degree of saving, a degree of investment, which will make purchasing power for the people that they did not have in the last war. In the last war money was, concentrated in the hands of the few who made a deal of money out of the war. They had tax-free bonds that do not exist at this time. I think our economic position will be much better than it was at that time.
You had better wait and see.

I wish to touch on another subject. We are at war. Nova Scotia was very vulnerable at the start of the war. There were many people who thought Nova Scotia might be in an invasion district. Many people thought our shores might be visited by the fleets and armies of our enemies. I wish to tell the committee that within sight of the shore of Nova Scotia merchant ships were sunk by submarines and the crews brought into our ports. We had the enemy right at our door. What kind of minister would it be who had regard for the national safety of this country who would put key industries such as munition factories and that kind of thing on the coast unless it was necessary for him to do so? One of the things we are told about Canada is that you can do things in comparative safety. The air force is in Canada because of its comparative safety owing to vast distances. In so far as some of the industries are concerned I am sure that the safety feature and the element of hazard were some of the things that came into play and should have come into play

The minister has intimate knowledge of Nova Scotia; I believe he is a descendant of the great Joe Howe, still the greatest of all Nova Scotians. Some years ago a little book called "The Liberal Way" was published, which contained a statement something to this effect: that a Liberal was one who was never satisfied, who always advanced and never arrived. That is the way I feel. We want to go on from one thing to another. We think we are doing fairly well; we consider that this war is being

run in a way that will commend itself to the thinking people of Canada; and we believe that these criticisms which are intended to disturb public opinion for political purposes are not worthy of men who have served for a long time in this House of Commons. That is a compliment to the hon. member for York-Sunbury. He is an able member of this house, who I believe could be, if he so desired, of great help to the minister. If anything is really wrong, let us hear about it and let us deal with it; but please let us not see the spirit which is sometimes manifest during the confusion of an election, when Canada is facing such severe conditions and when men should be doing their best in order that our industrial effort may be the utmost of which this country is capable.

I am sorry to say that I am not a descendant of Joe Howe, but I am very proud of the fact that Joe Howe and I come from common ancestors. I think that is the most I can claim in that connection.
