Last evening the hon. member for Lake Centre offered some comments on the wood fuel situation in Manitoba. I think his statement is pretty well summed up on page 1777 of Hansard, where he is reported as follows:
After all, when the minister speaks I listen to him, and he can answer me afterwards, as I do him. Just because the minister realizes that $800,000 or thereabouts was thrown away, naturally he becomes annoyed. He was warned about this, and his controller was warned that the wood was not needed in Winnipeg, that wood could have been obtained in Manitoba at a freight rate of 4J to 7 cents.
As I stated yesterday, the fact of the matter is that the situation last autumn was considered so serious that leave was sought to move the adjournment of the house to call the attention of the government to an alarming situation. The hon. J. S. McDiarmid, Minister of Mines and Natural Resources of Manitoba, predicted a wood fuel shortage of from 100,000 to 125,000 cords in that province for the winter of 1943-44. My department was responsible for the fuel situation, and took steps to provide 500,000 cords of emergency fuel wood, cut in such locations as could be arranged, and available to move into distressed areas. Fortunately we have had a mild winter, but the fact that we have had these

reserve stock-piles has saved a good many situations during the winter. If the winter had been severe I feel certain that we still would have met the need, but owing to the mild winter we have a considerable quantity of emergency wood available. As regards the Winnipeg situation, naturally if there was to be a shortage it would be at the end of the winter. The movement of 500,000 cords of wood involves the movement of about 350 cars of wood every day of the season, and that is a fair job for the railways. Naturally the wood had to be moved into strategic positions gradually; we could not wait until the actual shortage developed and then hope to get cars overnight to carry out the movement. Therefore in the early part of the winter we were moving certain quantities of wood into centres where we believed it would be required. Actually we moved 8,733 cords of poplar from the head of the lakes to Winnipeg. This wood was purchased at a cost of $7.50 a cord f.o.b. freight cars. The freight charges have averaged $5.18 a cord, based on an average rate of thirteen cents per 100 pounds. Sales have been made to dealers at $5.15 a cord, which has resulted in a loss to the government on the sale of this wood of approximately $65,700. I compare that figure with the figure mentioned by the hon. member for Lake Centre, namely, $S00,000. I believe his earlier figure was from $600,000 to $900,000, but apparently in the latter part of his remarks he compromised on $800,000, which is an exaggeration by some twelve or fourteen times.
My hon. friend says that he has no objection to wood being moved. He thinks it is quite proper to arrange for these emergency supplies, and to move them. But he said we should have waited until the wood had dried out, because we could have moved it at a lower freight rate. I point out to him that this wood was cut in the autumn, and it does not dry very well when it is frozen. Therefore to have moved it at the cheaper freight rate would have meant waiting twelve months, and moving it for the next year. Had the winter been cold, that would not have helped the situation in the city of Winnipeg during the present winter.
I think that covers the corrections. The hon. member for Lake Centre is an industrious member of parliament. But it seems to me that he spends too much time in speaking in the house, and too little time in acquiring the facts. I would suggest for his future guidance that he do a little more research, so that-

He does not need a lecture from the minister.

I am speaking now. I took a lecture from him last night, and now I will give him one, if he does not mind. Of course, if he minds I will stop.

Now that we have had the statement from the minister the facts have been revealed. The minister has referred to the 8,733 cords of the 75,000 cords that were cut at the head of the lakes. If the same proportion on the 75,000 cords was loss, then the loss would actually be about $600,000. Would the minister now tell us as to the disposal of the remaining 67,000 cords; where they were sold; how much was the cost, and what the freight rate was? If the computation is made in connection with the 75,000 cords, it will be found to be very close to my estimate. The figure I gave in regard to cost was correct, and in regard to the sale price of the wood-I said 12,500 cords-I was correct.
Now I ask him to give us the figure with reference to the other 67,000 cords. I do not think the suggestion made by the minister will be borne out by the facts. When I make a statement, and take a stand such as I have done from such information as I am able to gather, it is correct. I have not in any way made statements which are incorrect. In that connection let me say this, that one of the great difficulties hon. members have is that they must go outside the house to get information that should be readily available in the house. This can be secured only by members who are industrious enough to spend their time in investigating these matters. If any question were asked regarding this matter the same answer might very well have been given, one which has been given too often in the past, that it is not in the public interest. The investigation I made disclosed, and it is borne out by the figures submitted, that on the basis of 8,733 cords, the loss suffered by the government would be over $600,000.
Let me add this now, that the government sold this wood at $5.15 a cord. My figure of 12,500 cords was wrong. The government sold this, and there is no denial of the fact that the controller, and the fuel controller in Winnipeg, were not discouraged in making the sale, but went ahead with it. The individuals who purchased it for $5.15 a cord immediately turned it over in the ordinary course of events to the city of Winnipeg at $6 a cord.
Nothing of the kind.
I beg your pardon?
Absolute denial.
All right.
My hon. friend had better stop talking and let me tell him the facts.
Will the minister give us the facts as to what disposal was made of the 67,000 cords of wood, to account for the 75,000 cords?

A considerable part of the

minister said last night that some part of it was shipped east.

Probably some of it was; I will get the exact figure. A very considerable part of it is there, and will be moved by barge into the Toronto area during the summer months when, as suggested by the hon. member, it will be dried out. But my hon. friend is trying to dodge, very artfully. Last night he confined his remarks entirely to the scandal of moving wood into Winnipeg. If it is not worth that amount to make the city of Winnipeg secure against any eventuality in the matter of fuel wood, then perhaps we acted extravagantly in that matter. But, knowing what we do know, and having the alarming statements not only in this house, but from the provincial authorities in Winnipeg, I think we were justified in doing what we did do.

Hon. HUMPHREY MITCHELL (Minister of Labour) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Technical Education Act to make available, for the purposes of the act, any portion of the unexpended appropriation during the period of five years succeeding the fiscal year ending March 31, 1944.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps, before we go into committee, the minister might like to give some explanation to the house as to the reasons and necessity for the bill to be founded on this resolution. I would ask him if he is in a position to do so at this stage.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this resolution is precedent to the introduction of a bill to provide for the continuation of the provisions
Technical Education Act

of the Technical Education Act of 1919, as amended by the Technical Education Act of 1929 and again of 1934.
The scope of the proposed amendment is fully set out in the resolution. Similar resolutions were considered and similar bills passed by parliament in 1929, 1934 and 1939, in order to effect the continuance of the original act of 1919. Hon. members will remember that under the act the dominion government provided $10,000,000 for purposes of technical education throughout the dominion, $10,000 being provided yearly for each province and the remainder of the $10,000,000 being apportioned on the basis of population. Under the original act and subsequent amendments, twenty-five per cent of the money provided by the dominion and the provinces goes into building construction.

Yes, and seventy-five per cent to provide the necessary technical education. Every province with the exception of Manitoba has taken up its allotment of the $10,000,000, and at the moment there is $147,430.42 left in the allotment for Manitoba. All that this amendment does is to make possible the expenditure by the dominion of that amount in conjunction with the province of Manitoba.
I should like to point out to the house that the Department of Justice has indicated that the bill founded on this resolution must receive royal assent before the 31st of this month or else the original bill will lapse. speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPROPRIATION OF UNEXPENDED FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this resolution
affords an opportunity to the house to discuss one of the most important and, indeed, urgent questions facing the people of Canada at this time, a question which will become more important and more urgent perhaps as the days roll by. Apart altogether from the divisions into which the educational programmes of the provinces and the dominion fall, whether it be technical, vocational or some other branch of the educational field, this whole problem of education is one to which the house and the country should give urgent consideration.
One must, of course, approach the problem of education first of all from the point of view of the respective jurisdictions of the provinces and the dominion. Under the British North America Act, by section 93, education rests primarily with the provinces, and with that none of us will quarrel, because primarily it is a provincial matter and must remain with the provinces. But that does not presuppose that

there is not a responsibility for education resting also upon this dominion parliament within the jurisdiction in which it operates. Technical education particularly, and if one wishes to describe it, adult education and vocational training is not only of provincial but of federal concern, it being always borne in mind that the primary jurisdiction for education rests and must rest with the provinces.
The Technical Education Act passed, as the minister indicated, in 1919, was the beginning of that movement -which indicated the importance of technical education in a country like Canada, and more than that, it emphasized its importance from the dominion point of view. The importance of education and vocational training, if you like, is coming to be more and more clearly recognized as time goes on. We have made great strides in the educational field in the various provinces, but that does not mean that there is not still much to be done. The skills of the mind are important, but we must never lose sight of the importance of the training of the hand, and in this country in the days to come I hope that we shall always maintain a good balance as between the skills of the mind and the skills of the hand.
The problem of education has been tackled by the provinces, and by some of them very courageously. In Ontario from which I come there has been a recognition of the need for reforms in the educational system. The government of the Hon. George Drew has already during its short regime in this province recognized and will continue to recognize the importance of the educational system to the people of Ontario, and education is featured in the programme which that government is now attempting to carry out with great celerity and dispatch. Education is one of the planks on which that government was elected, clearly indicating the importance of the whole problem of education in the provincial sphere. Here is the programme of the province so far as education is concerned:
Our educational system will be completely revised so that every child in this province will have an opportunity to be educated to the full extent of their mental capacity, no matter where they live or what the financial circumstances of their parents may be. Vocational training will be made a much more important part of the school work, so that children may be prepared to earn a living by practical vocational instruction. The important place of our teachers in each community will be fully recognized.
I believe that to be a reflection of the general thought concerning educational affairs. Perhaps this is not the time or the place to discuss a subject which comes within the jurisdiction of the provinces; but we must recognize that it will be a responsibility within
\

Technical Education Act
the competence of the dominion to tackle, and fairly soon, those aspects of education which relate to matters of geography and ability to pay; to see to it that a student's location or his financial position shall not, as in the past, prejudice his right to a proper education. That is one of the ways in which the dominion and the dominion government can play an important part in the reform of our educational system. The question of ability to pay affects the whole problem of equal opportunity for our children. I am one who believes that the potential value to Canada of the boy or the girl in the far hinterlands is just as great as that of children who live in areas of greater opportunity, larger wealth, and more closely concentrated population. Having that definitely in mind, realizing the great differences of income which prevail in the different geographical locations and sections of Canada, I am frank to say that it does not seem right that because a child is born in one particular part of the country he should be denied full and equal opportunity so far as education goes. Attention must be given to the removal of the bars of geographical isolation and financial incapacity, so that the fullest measure of education shall be available to those who have the capacity and the desire to profit by it.
I hope that the government will also consider and review the whole matter of national scholarships. I realize that moves have been made in this respect. National scholarships would go far to meet a very real problem connected with education. I suppose there is cot one hon. member but can call to mind boys and girls who were brilliant and industrious and who desired to obtain an adequate education, but who, because of their parents' lack of means, or for other reasons beyond their control, were denied that opportunity. It seems to me that this nation cannot risk the loss of many bright minds merely because of such obstacles as I have mentioned, and which it is within the power of this parliament to remove.
Therefore, if the matter comes within the purview of the minister's department, I suggest to him that he enlarge the scheme and increase the amounts of national scholarships to enable students of this class to pursue their courses to the limits of their mental capacity rather than to the limits of their material resources.
The whole question of technical and vocational training assumes special importance because of the great job which will have to be done when our armed forces are demobilized'. Under particularly good leadership-I refer to the Canadian Legion-a great move
has heen made in the interests of the men of the armed forces while they are in the service. In addition, men benefit by the trades which they are enabled to learn while under enlistment. But I believe the government will have to consider enlarging the possibilities of giving young Canadians of both sexes, when they cease to wear the uniform, an education which will enable them not merely to become equal in earning capacity but to have even some preference over their civilian contemporaries and others who have not borne the brunt of battle through these years. In the matter of both technical and vocational education it is the dominion government which must give the lead and provide funds.
Adult education through the radio and the motion picture affords an important subject for consideration. In this field the federal government could properly take a heavy measure of responsibility. The air waves and the screen provide media particularly suited to this type of national education.
In passing, let me point out that in the rural communities there has not yet been developed, to the extent that we could wish, a proper system of education on agricultural lines, a system which through the primary and the secondary schools will train and equip our youth for agricultural activities. It is not impossible that many men in this chamber would now be engaged in agriculture instead of some other calling had it not been fashionable in the old days in the secondary schools for men-and women too-to drift into the professions. That trend, observable all over Canada, has not been a good thing for agriculture although it has enriched the larger centres. If agriculture is to continue to be a great industry and to develop as we hope, it is not too much to expect that our educational system shall direct and guide pupils from their early days into lines of agricultural activity and instil in them pride in the agricultural vocation. That is one of the things which must come in this land.
We have had debates in this house on the question of agricultural research, which, as most members who took part in those debates pointed out, is an important departure in that industry. In the competitive days to come no stone must be left unturned to ensure that farm life in Canada shall be raised to a position of importance so that it may take its place alongside other lines of endeavour and find its level of equality with other industries. The workers of Canada, too, are entitled to a broader and more abundant scheme which will be of benefit to their children, enabling them to obtain proper technical education and vocational training generally.
Technical Education Act

I merely wanted to point out on this occasion the importance of the whole problem of which this is but a very small part. Technical education, vocational training and education generally will, I hope, provide a means whereby this parliament, and the government, whatever government may succeed this one, shall make sure that the people are not neglected as in the past. We must see to that.

speechtext:
Of course, you are the only one who has ever suggested such a possibility. I am trying to be modest in the rather boastful air to the left of me. My hon. friend used to teach school, but after all he will not choose to regard me as a pupil at the moment. During the past in Canada education has been regarded by the dominion as an orphan. That must no longer be so. While we must respect and preserve and maintain at all times full provincial jurisdiction in this matter, still there are many fields in which we as a federal parliament can assist the various parts of the dominion financially as they need assistance. I am not one who believes that simply by giving grants to the provinces we as a dominion should hold a bludgeon over the provincial legislatures to make them do what we would like to have them do. That must never be the policy of the government. Rather, it must be the policy of this government and parliament to see that financial assistance is given to the provinces so as to provide a more uniform opportunity to pupils across Canada, regardless of the financial condition into which they were bom or in which perhaps their parents may find themselves.
I would urge the minister to regard this measure as simply one of those factors, small as it may be, in the general scheme which I hope the government is planning in the way of assistance to education throughout the dominion. The challenge to this parliament and to this government, the challenge to all the provinces, is imperative. The education of the new generation which is coming up is of such vast importance as almost to stagger one sometimes when one stops to contemplate the possibilities. In Europe and in other parts of the world education has been directed along certain lines which we think are undemocratic and which have led to bitter trouble throughout the world. The new generation now growing up are our citizens of to-morrow and are the most valuable asset that Canada possesses. There is no asset that can equal our pupils, and we must recognize this fact. Moreover, we must treat with equal consideration those charged1 with the responsibility of teach-

ing those pupils. They also are valuable national assets. The teaching profession, however, has not been paid as it should have been. We have money for other lines of endeavour but there has been too niggardly treatment of our teachers. I hope, therefore, that in the days which lie ahead there will be something better for those who teach and those who would learn, and that a giant structure, erected with a greater Canada in view, will make for that progress and development to which we all look forward.
I have pleasure, therefore, in supporting tonight the minister's resolution upon which a bill respecting technical education is to be founded. I regard it as a channel whereby we can bring to the government's attention the important problem of education, which must no longer be ignored or disregarded.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPROPRIATION OF UNEXPENDED FUNDS
speechtext:
I am not going to hold up the passage of this resolution or the bill that will be based upon it; nevertheless I do not believe that this is a step in our progress toward better education for everyone. Indeed, it is only a small part of a plan that was put into effect many years ago. One of the provinces has failed to take advantage of its share of the assistance granted, but I see no reason why the house should not pass the bill so as to give the province concerned an opportunity to take advantage of such assistance if it wishes to do so. I should like to impress upon the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) my belief that the time is opportune for the government, of which he is a member, to bring before the house a comprehensive scheme of federal assistance to education.
I am sure the minister and hon. members generally will agree with me that such assistance is badly needed in Canada. The mere fact that of the nine provinces that had the opportunity of benefiting under this legislation, which was passed in 1919, eight have long ago taken advantage of the assistance offered to further technical education in their respective areas, indicates to me that the provinces would welcome additional assistance. I agree with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) that there is no reason why the dominion, in giving assistance, should seek more supervision than would be necessary to make sure that the grant was properly used. It was not found difficult to accept the grant and to satisfy both the provinces and the dominion under the old plan. I believe that many of the technical schools in the country are benefiting to-day from government assistance given for the purpose of training boys and girls in war work. I submit to you. Mr. MARCH 24, 1944
Technical Education Act
Speaker, that if it is important-and we agree it is important-to train boys and girls for war, it is equally important, nay, more important, to train boys and girls for peace as soon as the war is over. The problems of peace, as the years preceding the war brought home to us so definitely, are no less important than the problems of war.
There is another reason why the government should be ready with a comprehensive scheme of federal assistance for education once peace comes. But may I repeat, I see no reason why it should not be put into effect before peace comes. This war has taken an enormous toll of the better educated young men of this and of every other nation engaged in it. Possibly there has been no other war in history where the flower of the intelligence of our young people, if I am using the correct term, has been sacrificed to the same extent as in this war. Unfortunately in the past only a very small number of our people were able, to any extent, to take advantage of advanced educational training. I had the figures for British Columbia a few years ago. The figures that I shall give may not be absolutely accurate, but I think they will be found to be very close to the mark. It is doubtful if seventy-five per cent of the pupils who begin school at the age of five or six go through the elementary schools, and not more than thirty-five or forty per cent enter high school. Only a percentage of the number entering high school continue to matriculation. In British Columbia statistics show that only four per cent of the pupils who go to school reached university and a still smaller percentage than that passed through university. Surely we are not on that low intellectual level that only four per cent of our people can benefit by a university education?
There are various reasons why we have made such a poor showing in our schools. The reasons are largely economic. First of all, there is the poverty of some of the provinces. Then there is the poverty of certain districts within the province where, under our provincial educational system, the school districts pay for the elementary education with, of course, a certain amount of provincial assistance. Then there is the greatest drawback of all, the poverty in the home. Until we raise the economic level of our people by increasing wages, or in some other way, poverty will continue to be a bar to the education of the families of the poor. I do not think that difficulty can be met by scholarships. I believe that scholarships are of value; but the capacity of the pupil to benefit by advanced
education cannot be measured until that pupil has a least reached high school and has possibly had some years in high school. Therefore there must be something more than scholarships. Some means must be provided by which the children of the poor can be continued in school until it can be discerned whether or not they can benefit by further education.
As I said at the beginning, I see no reason why this measure should not be allowed to pass without any great amount of discussion, but I believe this house should impress upon the minister the urgent necessity of the government doing something to give assistance to the provinces to further technical and other advanced education. This would in turn take some of the load off the provinces and more could be spent on elementary education. But there is a whole field here that will have to be covered in some way if we are to do some of the things that the leader of the opposition said should be done, but which were never done, regardless of what party was in power in Canada.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): I have listened with great pleasure to the speeches made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Graydon) and the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis).
This resolution precedes a measure to amend the Technical Education Act. There is not an hon. member who will not agree that education, especially technical education, is an important thing for youth. But while I was listening to the speeches I was thinking of something, namely, that it is very good to boost education on paper and even in legislation, but on the other hand we must be more practical than that. We must not take it for granted that the men who will indulge in technical work shall be men who are physically unfit. At the present time those who work as technical tradesmen are considered as making an inferior contribution to the war effort. They are not put on the same footing as the men and women in the army. If all that has been said before is true, it must be acknowledged that those men who work in technical trades do something that is just as vital to the war effort as that done by those who are in the army.
That is my first contention. Now it is the fashion to give the cold shoulder to the man in overalls. Many people are under the impression that sick boys from sanatoria, boys who have been undernourished and who are weak physically, can do the work of ablebodied men. I do not agree; probably no one does in private, but when the time comes
Technical Education Act

to express an opinion everyone seems afraid to say so. There is no shame in wearing overalls; there is no shame in having spots of grease on overalls. The beautiful and expensive limousines in which landlords ride among the crowds of pedestrians are built by men who have greasy spots on their overalls; the landlords have none. The man who sweats tailoring fine uniforms for those who occupy high posts in the army is unknown. It reminds me of a reception; it is not the cook or chef who is complimented, it is the host. A caterer told me that every time he saw a fine cake he thought of the perspiration of the man who had looked after the baking of that cake.
It seems to me, sir, that in times like these people express views which are not exactly those they hold in the bottom of their hearts. Because I speak like this I may be told that I am opposed to the education of youth, that I am opposed to a federal grant to aid1 technical education. I want to respect the constitution and the law. In the Sirois report I saw a lengthy memorandum about federal gifts to the provinces in aid of education. According to the British North America Act, which is considered by some of my hon. friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party to be an obstacle to progress, education is under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces. Why? The reason is obvious; it is that education needs an immediate rather than a remote control. I give every credit to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), but how can he possibly supervise the education of young Canadian boys and girls throughout this country? It is hard for a provincial minister of education to do that within his own province; so how would it be possible for the minister to do it for all of Canada?
That is my second point. My third point is that the best help the Minister of Labour can give to youth in technical trades is to keep in those trades the young men who are doing well at the present time, making armaments, making munitions, making clothes for the soldiers, working on the farms, on the railways and in the railway shops. Not long ago the railways decided to make an agreement with the Department of National Defence, in virtue of which young men with experience in technical trades, who have filled positions requiring experience both on the railways and in the shops, could not have any further postponement of military service. Though they had years of experience as tradesmen and only a few months of experience as soldiers, they were told, "You are soldiers first. We will not
[Mr. Pouliotd
ask you to continue at the trade in which you have acquired special skill. Go into the army." Well, sir, before voting money to encourage the training of young men in technical trades, I think first we should acknowledge the importance of those trades, and not give the cold shoulder to tradesmen and men in overalls. We should recognize officially that in war time these men do not help the country only by subscribing to war bonds; they help by their work, by their sweat, and by their activities in the various fields in which they are engaged. That is my point of view; and if this resolution is timely, there is no excuse whatever for not paying a special tribute of admiration to those men who work day and night in order to clothe the army, to arm those who are in it, to furnish them with munitions, food and transportation.

There must also be greater progress made in work of helping the students who enter our schools to find out what their latent and inherent talents, abilities and skills are. Then we must provide them with an opportunity to use those skills and talents to the best possible advantage. Every person differs, of course, and what is an education for one is not suitable as an education for another. But each has capacities which must be developed, and our educational system in this country has failed to find within our people their respective talents and capacities. There are people who can take tremendous advantage of a technical education, and there are others to whom it would be worthless. There must be an opportunity provided throughout all our nation for every person who has ability and talents to discover and use them.
The second point I wish to make is that there must exist in the minds of those who are getting an education the thought that when they have completed their education and training an opportunity will exist for them. They must have a feeling of security; there must be freedom from fear. We watched the youth of our nation graduate from our schools and colleges in 1930 to 1939 and go into the ranks of the unemployed, and then into the bread-line asking for relief. That must never happen again.
Canada can never fulfill her destiny until every child1 knows what his or her capacities and abilities are and has an opportunity to use them, not entirely for his or her own

While I agree wholeheartedly with the view of the previous speaker (Mr. Douglas, Weyburn) with respect to the effect which this resolution has upon the act itself, I shall not endeavour to go beyond the limitations which you, sir, have set.
We realize that this resolution has been brought forward with the express purpose of making available to Manitoba certain moneys which it has not used heretofore. I hope that Manitoba will recognize in the action which parliament is taking in this regard the fact that in that province, as a consequence of war, many establishments have been set up which, following their usefulness for war purposes, may well be utilized in connection with technical education. Moreover, I hope that Manitoba will recognize that as a result of the
specialized type of training which we are giving to-day to many of our service personnel, we shall before very long have an abundance of fully qualified instructors to carry on technical educational work in that province. What I say of Manitoba in that regard applies equally well to the other Canadian provinces.
I trust that Manitoba will recognize, together with all the other provinces, that in order to maintain fully qualified and competent technical instructors it must be prepared to recognize the importance of that type of work and to pay salaries which will induce these people to take a more intense interest in that type of instruction work and, therefore, add greatly to technical education in that province.
There is a good deal that I could say, but let me just add this:	Not only must we
concentrate upon providing technical education for the purpose of enabling young people to earn a living, but we must so educate them as to enable them to make profitable use of their spare time. I think we have almost entirely overlooked that in connection with our techincal education in the past. I agree with this resolution wholeheartedly, Mr. Speaker, as do the other members of this group.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPROPRIATION OF UNEXPENDED FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this resolution is to make available to the province of Manitoba money provided by the federal government to encourage technical education, which offer Manitoba did not accept in years gone by. I shall certainly support the principle of this resolution, because I think it is a good thing to help technical education throughout Canada.
There is another reason why I am supporting this resolution. It is that it will create a precedent which may be very beneficial to my own province of Quebec, where the same situation exists in connection with old age pensions. For nearly ten years sums were provided by the federal government to help pay the cost of-old age pensions throughout Canada, but the province of Quebec did not take advantage of that offer. Perhaps, following this precedent, Quebec may be able to ask this government for the share of the money provided for all provinces for that purpose which it did not claim in previous years, and that, of course, would be of great benefit to the province of Quebec.

Any portion of the ten million dollars appropriated under the act which may remain unexpended at the expiration of the fiscal year one thousand nine hundred and thirty-nine, whether previously carried forward or not, shall be carried forward and remain available according to its apportionments for the purposes of this act during any one or more of the five succeeding fiscal years, and no portion of the said ten million dollars shall be paid to any province after the thirty-fist day of March, one thousand nine hundred and forty-four.

Any portion of the ten million dollars appropriated under the act which may remain unexpended at the expiration of the fiscal year one thousand nine hundred and thirty-nine. . . .

speechtext: Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of bill No. 35, to amend the Exchequer Court Act.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF THIRD JUDGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before this bill is read a second time I have one or two observations to make.
First of all, I should like to bring to the minister's attention the situation in connection with the Exchequer Court of Canada. At the present time I think there will be few who will disagree with the proposal in this bill to increase the membership of the court. I am hopeful that the minister, when he closes the debate on the second reading or during the committee stage, will indicate to the house whether there is not more behind the passing of this legislation perhaps than appears on the surface. I wish to raise my voice to-night in protest against what I think is fairly close to what the public believe is almost a national disgrace. I refer to a certain type of legislation that sometimes finds its way into the Senate and House of Commons. I refer to the time-honoured subject of divorce. I am not going to deal with it in any detail to-night. Suggestions have been made from time to time seeking to rid the two chambers of parliament of the scourge of having to deal with this type of legislation from year to year. I think most hon. members are agreed that if there is some sensible, sane way of having divorce dealt

Exchequer Court Act
with other than by a private bill in parliament, it is our duty and bounden obligation to find that better means and method.
It seems to me that the best method would be to refer the question of divorce to the Exchequer Court of Canada. That has been suggested already by my colleague, the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson), at a previous stage of this session. I repeat, with all the emphasis at my command, that I am hopeful that the government will delay no longer with respect to this matter, because not only is this house but, I suggest, the other place, too, sick and tired, if I may use an expression of the street, of dealing with divorce legislation in parliament. There is no justification, to my way of thinking, for continuing the present situation any longer. Perhaps this increase in the membership of the exchequer court is proposed for the reason that the court may deal with this very subject. I hope that the minister will give due consideration to that suggestion and that an end will speedily be put to parliament having to deal with this type of legislation. I think most decent people who are sent here by their constituents rebel against the hearing of evidence and all that is involved in this type of legislation. That is all I shall say at the moment, but there is so much to be said that perhaps on some other occasion, when the government sees fit, the matter may be further discussed.
There is a second point I wish to raise in the brief observations I have to make, namely, with reference to the way in which the exchequer court works. I can quite see that the minister may have been forced into the position of proposing an increase in the membership of the court largely because of the situation which has grown up in the court wherein there are delays with respect to legislation and the delivery of judgment. Most of the legislation affecting the people of this country at this time has never seen parliament. I would point out, Mr. Chairman, that it is eleven o'clock, if the minister wants to discuss the bill further. Is my voice getting so weak that I cannot be heard? I am suggesting that it is eleven o'clock, Mr. Chairman.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I have no other observations to offer on this point, unless there are other questions it is felt I should answer.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-Power to appoint a deputy judge.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF THIRD JUDGE
speechtext:
There are a number of questions we have to ask and it is now past eleven o'clock, Mr. Chairman.
Section stands.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver Centre) the house adjourned at 11:10 pun.
Monday, March 27, 1944
